en: One should not commit any evil in the entire world by means of mind, speech, or body;
empty of desires, mindful and clearly comprehending, one should not pursue suffering which leads to misfortune.
Beings who perceive what is to be told are established in this very thing that is to be told.
Without fully understanding that which is to be told, they fall into the power of death.
But having fully understood that which is to be told, one does not conceive of a speaker;
for that by which others might speak of him no longer exists for such a person. (Śag 2.1–2)
He who considers himself equal, superior, or even inferior would engage in dispute with him;
but for one who does not waver in these three states, there exists neither equality nor superiority.
Having severed craving for name-and-form in this world and having abandoned pride, he does not enter into attachment.

Neither in the world of gods and humans, nor here within, nor outside, did they see him— his smoke extinguished, free from affliction, and devoid of desire. Because my mind is overwhelmed by sensual passion, it burns with fever.
"Come now, Gautama, out of compassion, speak peace to me!
Your mind is being consumed by a perception based on error;
therefore, abandon the sign associated with passion for the beautiful."
Always cultivate the meditation on the foul with one-pointedness and perfect composure;
quickly extinguish the fire of passion, lest you be burned again and again.
Behold the conditioned factors as inferior, as suffering, and likewise as non-self.
Having established mindfulness directed toward the body, be full of disenchantment. Cultivate the signless, which destroys the underlying tendencies of pride;
then, through the realization of pride, you will bring an end to suffering.
The Maiden’s Question Verse:

How does a monk, dwelling much in what way, cross over the sixth flood after having crossed the five? How does one who meditates, having crossed the vast thirst for sensual pleasures, remain without the tether of rebirth? (Śag 4.1)
With body tranquil and mind well-liberated, acting without volitional effort, mindful and unshakable,
having fully understood the Dharma and dwelling in meditation free from discursive thought, he is devoid of anger, longing, sloth, and faults.
A monk who frequently dwells in such a state has crossed the five floods and crosses over the sixth here in this world.
Meditating thus, he crosses over the vast thirst for sensual desires, having let go of the tether.
For this world is constantly terrified, and these beings are perpetually anxious,
whether sufferings have not yet arisen or have already arisen again.

If there is anything you have not yet spoken of when questioned, tell that to me. O divine one, I see no liberation other than through knowledge and austerity, other than through the restraint of the senses, and other than through the renunciation of everything.

"Ah, after a long time indeed, I behold a brahmin who has attained final nirvana, who has transcended all enmity and fear, and who has crossed over the worldly attachments. By whom has this people been led to excellence, and by whom has the path leading to liberation been set forth? Śag 5.3.
Established where and training where does this mortal man not fear the next world?

(Śag 6.1) He who possesses virtue, possesses knowledge, has cultivated the self, is concentrated, mindful, and upright—for him all the fevers of sorrow are abandoned, he whose mind is rightly mindful and liberated. (Śag 6.2)
By him the people have been led to excellence, and the path leading to liberation has been set forth.
Abiding in this and training in this, this mortal person does not fear the world beyond.
How does one become renowned? How does one come to possess wealth?
How does one attain renown? How does one find friends?
Through ethical conduct one becomes famous; through generosity one becomes possessed of enjoyments.
Through truthfulness one attains renown; by giving, one finds friends.

Where indeed name-and-form are completely brought to an end,
there the streams turn back and the path does not proceed; there,
in this world, suffering and pleasure are completely brought to an end.
By what does one cross the flood? By what does one cross the ocean?
By what does one abandon suffering? And by what is one purified? (Śag 9.1) For by faith one crosses the flood, and by heedfulness one crosses the ocean.
Through vigor one abandons suffering; through wisdom one becomes completely pure.
Who crosses this flood day and night without weariness?
And who does not sink into the deep, which is without support and without standing ground?
Endowed with virtue in every respect, possessed of wisdom, well-composed,
reflecting inwardly, and mindful, he crosses over this world so difficult to cross.
Detached from the perceptions of sensual desire, he transcends the fetter of form.

He does not sink in that which is without support, without foundation, and profound. “O Blessed One, what is the cause of passion and hatred? From where do aversion and delight arise, and from whence comes this horripilation? And from what do the mental discursive thoughts originate, that they take refuge in the youth as children do in a nurse? (Śag 10.3–11.1)

Born of attachment and produced from the self, like the shoots from the trunk of a banyan tree, they are separately clinging to sensual pleasures, like the *mālatī* creeper or other vines in the forest.
Passion and hatred arise from this source; from this comes discontent and delight, and the bristling of the hair.
And the mental discursive thoughts arising from this [mind] rely upon it, just as children rely upon a nursemaid.
O Yakṣa, those people who understand them and their underlying cause dispel them;
they cross over the ocean of this flood, which was never crossed before, so that there is no further rebirth.
This is the task for a Brahmin who is untiring:
the complete abandonment of desires, for he no longer craves existence. He has the task of a Brahmin; indeed, a Brahmin is said to be one who has accomplished his purpose.
As long as one does not find a firm footing, one struggles with all one's limbs until reaching the shore;
but having reached the shore here, one stands upon dry land and no longer struggles—one who has gone to the further shore is thus called "liberated.
Dāma, this is the simile for the Brahmin whose taints are exhausted, who is wise and an attainer of meditative concentration.
All his fevers of grief have been abandoned, for his mind is rightly mindful and liberated. (Geya:
O monk, O monk, you have crossed the flood!
"Yes, O goddess;
in that which is without support and without foundation, you have crossed the flood.
Yes, O goddess."
"In what way, monk, did you cross the flood when there is no support and no foothold? "O goddess, in whatever way I exert myself, in that very way I sink;
in whatever way I sink, in that very way I come to rest."
"In whatever way I remain established, in that very way I am carried along;
in whatever way, O deity, I do not exert myself, in that very way I do not sink"—thus should the white side (the path of purification) be understood in detail.

Alone, you wander in the forest, meditating—either deprived of wealth or seeking it; have you perhaps incurred some debt for something belonging to the village? Why do you not form friendships with people? You have no friendship with anyone at all. (Śag 14.1)

"Through the non-attainment of worldly objects, there is peace for the heart here; having conquered this army that appears so pleasant and charming, I, meditating alone, have experienced happiness. Therefore, I do not form friendship with people;
no friendship exists for me with anyone. (Śag 14.2)
Impermanent indeed are conditioned phenomena, subject to the nature of arising and passing away;
for having arisen, they cease—their subsiding is bliss.
Heedfulness is the state of immortality; heedlessness is the state of death.
The heedful do not die; the heedless, however, are always as if dead.
For a person who is agitated by discursive thoughts, possessed of intense passion, and who perceives beauty [in the impure], craving increases further; it makes his bondage firm.
People hold dear one who abides in the Dharma, who is perfected in virtue, modest, truthful,
and who does what is pleasing to themselves.
Having seen here in this world the evil consequences of actions directed toward others, one should reflect upon them.

One should not do that oneself, for one who is bound by such actions is wicked. (Śag 19; cf. Uv 9.6) The Noble Ones say that well-spoken words are supreme: one should speak what is pleasant and not what is unpleasant—that is the second [quality].
One should speak the truth and not falsehood—that is the third. One should speak according to the Dharma and not against the Dharma—that is the fourth. (Śag 20; cf. Uv 8.11)
Faith, then modesty, virtue, and also generosity—these qualities are praised by the noble ones.
For they call this the path leading to heaven; by it, indeed, one goes to the world of the gods.
Having heard the Dharma, one understands it; having heard it, one turns away from evil.
Having heard [the truth], one abandons what is harmful; having heard it, one attains nirvāṇa.
Like space, he is unstained; like a pillar of Indra, he does not waver.
Like a lake filled with mud, the wise man does not delight in saṃsāra.
Those people who judge me by my form and follow me by my voice,
being under the sway of desire and passion, do not know me.
One may understand the internal, yet one does not see the external.

He who perceives only internal results is indeed led away by mere sound. He who does not know the internal yet perceives only the external—he too is led away by mere sound. (Śag 24.2–3; cf. Uv 22.13–14)
He who does not know within and does not see without,
the fool who is obstructed on all sides— he too is led away by sound.
But he who knows within and sees without...

The steadfast one, possessing wisdom regarding the means of escape, is not led away by mere sound. While the sixth lord, the king, is being stained by passion, the one who is free from passion remains unstained; the fool is said to be the one who is impassioned.
The city has bones for its ramparts and sinews and flesh for its plaster;
therein lust, hatred, pride, and hypocrisy take their stand.
Just as a tortoise withdraws its limbs within its shell, so should a monk restrain the discursive thoughts of the mind.

Independent, not harming others, and having attained final nirvāṇa, he would not disparage anyone. Releasing both the equal and the unequal, as well as all arising and the formative forces of existence, the Sage— delighting in the internal and concentrated— burst forth like a bird from its eggshell.
There is no mire equal to desire; there is no seizure equal to hatred;
there is no net equal to delusion; there is no river equal to craving.
Indeed, there is no footprint in the sky, and there is no ascetic among outsiders.

Fools delight in conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), whereas the Tathāgatas are free from proliferation. He for whom neither stability nor proliferation exists, who has transcended both the tether and the bolt—
neither the world with its gods nor any other knows that thirstless Sage as he wanders.

He whose discursive thoughts have been shaken off, who is inwardly free from conceptualization, and who has completely transcended attachment and the perception of form—he, having departed from the four bonds, does not undergo birth.
Merit increases for one who gives; enmity is not accumulated by one who practices restraint.

The virtuous one abandons evil; through the destruction of the afflictions, he is at peace. To refrain from all evil, to attain what is wholesome, and to thoroughly subdue one’s own mind—this is the instruction of the Buddhas.

It is good to tame the mind, which is difficult to restrain, fickle, and falling wherever it pleases; a tamed mind brings happiness. One who is skilled in the signs of the mind experiences the flavor of seclusion.
Meditating, prudent, and mindful, he enjoys a spiritual joy and happiness free from worldly taints.

One who does not live by a craft, who is light, self-contented, and has conquered his senses; who is completely liberated, homeless, without the sense of "mine," and free from expectations; having abandoned desires, he wanders alone—he is a true monk.
"He who tames the mind—which travels far, wanders alone, is bodiless, and dwells in the cave, and which is difficult to tame—I call him a brahmin. (Śag 38; cf. Uv 33.55).
This concludes the "Questions of Ajita" from the *Pārāyaṇa*.

"By what is this world shrouded? By what does it not shine forth? What do you call its defilement, and what is its great fear? "The world is shrouded by ignorance; it does not shine forth because of negligence."
I say that attachment to talk is suffering; it brings great fear.
Streams flow everywhere; what is the obstruction of those streams?
Tell me the restraint of the streams: by what means are the streams blocked?
Whatever streams there are in the world, mindfulness is their damming;
I call this the restraint of the streams, for by wisdom they are closed up.
And of both wisdom and mindfulness, as well as of name-and-form, [there is the cessation] in every respect.
"Tell me, being asked this by me: where does all this cease?
Wisdom and mindfulness, as well as name-and-form in their entirety—through the cessation of consciousness, indeed, all this ceases here."
"How is it that for one who acts with mindfulness, consciousness is brought to cessation?
Being asked this, explain it to me exactly as it is, without doubt. [The Buddha replied:
"For one who does not delight in feeling, whether internal or external..."

For one who acts thus with mindfulness, consciousness is brought to cessation. O worthy sir, being asked, please explain to me the conduct of those who have mastered the Dharma and those various types of trainees, as it was practiced by the diligent one.
One should not be greedy for sensual pleasures; one should remain undisturbed in mind.
Skilled in all dharmas and mindful, a bhikṣu should wander forth. These are the verses concerning sensual pleasures from the *Arthavargīya*:

If that which is desired by one who longs for sensual pleasures succeeds, that mortal certainly becomes joyful in mind, having obtained what he sought. (Śag 40.1) If, for that person who longs for sensual pleasures and has given rise to desire...

Those desires fall away from him, and he suffers as if pierced by a thorn. He who completely abandons desires, like one treading upon the head of a serpent, is said to have transcended this clinging to the world.
If a man greedily covets fields, property, gold, cattle, horses, jewels, earrings, women, and slaves— each according to his own desire—
the powerful floods crush him, whether he be weak or strong. (Śag 40.4)
Then suffering follows him, just as water enters a leaking boat.
But for one by whom this [craving] has been utterly cut off and destroyed like the top of a palmyra tree,
sorrows turn away from him like a drop of water from a lotus leaf.
Śag_40.6 (cf. Uv 10.13ab and 3.10cd) The Stanza on the Auspicious Night (Bhadra-rātrīya):
One should not pursue the past, nor should one long for the future;
regarding those phenomena that have arisen in the present, the wise person, observing them here and there,
should cultivate that which is unassailable and unshakeable.
